paragraphs: Spatial experiments must account for relationships between locations when estimating causal effects. Treatment at one location can affect outcomes elsewhere, while outcomes at nearby locations can also be correlated. This paper studies how to design experiments around both features so that the resulting data provide more information and support more accurate causal estimates.

The proposed method constructs a surrogate for the estimator’s mean squared error, a measure of estimation accuracy. This substitute objective makes the design problem accessible to classical graph cut algorithms. The central contribution is therefore a connection between statistical design quality and an efficient computational procedure for choosing the design.

The approach accommodates moderate to large interference effects and adapts to different spatial covariance functions, which describe how outcomes vary together across space. The authors support the design with theoretical results and numerical experiments using synthetic environments and a city-scale ridesharing dispatch simulator. These findings support jointly considering interference and correlation when choosing spatial experimental designs.
icml-2025-balancing-interference-and-cor.tldr: A graph cut approach designs spatial experiments around both treatment spillovers and correlated outcomes to improve causal estimation.

paragraphs: An agent adapting to a new task needs observations that reveal what that task requires. Existing context-based offline meta-reinforcement learning methods often assume those observations come from task-specific behavior or repeated collection. CERTAIN examines the more demanding situation in which a policy must gather useful context in a single attempt, motivated by efficiency and safety.

The authors identify two obstacles: context can be ambiguous across tasks, and newly collected observations can differ from the training distribution. Their method uses heteroscedastic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty that varies with the context, to identify both problems. It then trains a context-collection policy that accounts for this uncertainty when gathering information for adaptation.

CERTAIN can be incorporated into classification, reconstruction, and contrastive learning approaches to task representation. Benchmark evaluations report improvements of up to 36% for one-shot adaptation and up to 34% for zero-shot adaptation over existing methods. These are maximum reported gains, supporting the value of learning how to collect informative context alongside learning how to interpret it.
icml-2025-certain-context-uncertainty-aw.tldr: CERTAIN uses context-dependent uncertainty to improve information collection and adaptation when an agent gets only one opportunity to gather context.

paragraphs: Referring multimodal language models answer questions about an indicated image region. Their responses can go wrong when a nearby or visually similar region draws attention away from the intended target. CPCF addresses this specific source of error by comparing responses associated with the target against responses associated with potentially misleading regions.

The framework generates outputs using both the supplied visual prompt and contrastive prompts drawn from distracting areas. Comparing those outputs helps suppress information that comes from outside the target. A prompt extraction network automatically identifies useful contrastive prompts, making the choice of distracting regions part of the method itself.

CPCF also includes self-training with unlabeled data to improve training quality and a distillation approach to reduce the extra computation required by contrastive decoding. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance. The findings support using explicit comparisons between image regions to improve response specificity, while the additional training and distillation components address the quality and efficiency of that comparison process.
icml-2025-cpcf-a-cross-prompt-contrastiv.tldr: CPCF compares responses to target and distracting image regions to make multimodal models answer more accurately about the intended region.

paragraphs: CVE-Bench measures whether language-model agents can exploit vulnerabilities in real web applications. The authors argue that existing evaluations either rely on abstract Capture-the-Flag challenges or provide incomplete coverage. Their benchmark instead uses critical-severity vulnerabilities recorded in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures system, grounding the evaluation in documented application weaknesses.

Building this evaluation requires reproducing vulnerable applications and assessing attacks whose behavior may be unpredictable. CVE-Bench provides a sandbox framework in which agents interact with vulnerable web applications under conditions intended to resemble real deployments. The framework also evaluates whether the attempted exploits succeed, connecting agent behavior to concrete outcomes.

In the reported experiments, the state-of-the-art agent framework exploits up to 13% of the benchmark’s vulnerabilities. This result demonstrates successful exploitation within the tested sandbox scenarios; it is not an estimate for all web vulnerabilities. The contribution is a way to measure this capability against realistic application flaws, alongside empirical evidence of the capabilities achieved in that setting.
icml-2025-cve-bench-a-benchmark-for-ai-a.tldr: CVE-Bench evaluates AI agents on real web application vulnerabilities, with a tested agent framework exploiting up to 13% of them.

paragraphs: Personalized treatment recommendations become difficult when there are many treatment options but relatively few observations for each. Differences in patient characteristics across treatment groups further complicate comparisons. This paper proposes combining similar treatments into groups before learning an individualized recommendation rule, while adjusting for those differences in patient characteristics.

The method uses calibration weights to balance covariates across treatment groups and a penalized working model to fuse similar treatments. Its double robustness concerns recovery of the underlying treatment groups: that recovery holds when either the calibration model or the outcome model is correctly specified. Practitioners can then apply treatment-rule learning methods within the fused treatment space.

The authors establish consistency, an oracle property for treatment fusion, and regret bounds for combinations with methods such as policy trees. Simulations show improved group recovery and policy value compared with existing approaches. An application uses electronic health record data from patients with two related blood cancers. Allowing a subset of covariates in subsequent policy learning also provides flexibility for addressing practical concerns such as fairness.
icml-2025-doubly-robust-fusion-of-many-t.tldr: A doubly robust procedure groups similar treatments and balances patient characteristics to support personalized recommendations when treatment options are numerous.

paragraphs: Generating a 3D object from text does not automatically produce something people prefer. DreamDPO addresses this gap by making preference information part of the optimization process for the 3D representation. Its objective is to improve both the quality of generated content and the ability to steer it toward desired characteristics.

The framework first creates pairs of examples. Reward models or large multimodal models then assess whether those pairs align with human preferences. A preference-based loss uses the resulting comparisons to update the 3D representation. This makes relative judgments between alternatives the main guidance signal, reducing dependence on precise absolute assessments of quality.

The approach matters because preference comparisons provide a way to guide fine-grained changes during generation. The authors report state-of-the-art experimental results, with higher-quality and more controllable 3D content than existing methods. These findings support the use of direct preference optimization for text-to-3D generation, with model-based preference assessment serving as the connection between candidate outputs and the optimization objective.
icml-2025-dreamdpo-aligning-text-to-3d-g.tldr: DreamDPO optimizes text-generated 3D content using pairwise preference judgments to improve quality and controllability.

paragraphs: Symbolic music generation faces a demanding combination of limited training data and the need for precise note pitches. A generated piece also needs to reflect the composer’s intentions to be useful in controlled creation. This paper introduces Fine-Grained Guidance, or FGG, as an efficient way to steer diffusion models toward those musical requirements.

FGG guides generation to align more closely with expert composers’ control and intent. The authors connect this guidance to accuracy, listenability, and overall musical quality. The intended applications include improvisation and interactive creation, where a system must support active musical direction rather than merely produce an unconstrained sequence.

The paper provides theoretical characterizations of both the difficulties of symbolic music generation and the effects of its guidance method. Numerical experiments and subjective evaluation support the approach’s effectiveness. A demonstration also supports real-time interactive generation. Together, these contributions connect an analysis of the generation problem with a control mechanism and evaluations that address both technical behavior and perceived musical results.
icml-2025-efficient-fine-grained-guidanc.tldr: Fine-Grained Guidance steers diffusion-based symbolic music generation toward composers’ intentions, with theoretical and experimental support.

paragraphs: Giving a language model more computation while answering often requires another model to evaluate its candidate responses or reasoning steps. JETTS asks whether language models that generate judgments and critiques are effective evaluators for this purpose. Their success in automatic evaluation does not by itself establish that they help generators improve during inference.

The benchmark covers mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following. It tests three uses of judges: reranking complete responses, selecting intermediate steps through beam search, and guiding revisions with critiques. The evaluation includes 10 judge models with 7–70 billion parameters and eight generator models with 6.7–72 billion parameters.

The results differ across these settings. Judges are competitive with outcome reward models when reranking responses, but consistently trail process reward models in step-level beam search. Their natural-language critiques are also ineffective at improving generator responses in the reported evaluation. The findings show why evaluator selection should account for its role in the inference procedure, rather than treating judging ability as a single transferable capability.
icml-2025-evaluating-judges-as-evaluator.tldr: JETTS finds that LLM judges can rerank responses competitively but struggle with step-level search and critique-guided improvement.

paragraphs: Event cameras record individual brightness changes asynchronously instead of capturing conventional image frames. Their imaging mechanism offers advantages for fast motion and challenging lighting, but an out-of-focus lens can still produce defocus blur. Sparse event data also make existing focusing algorithms difficult to apply efficiently. EvFocus tackles the reconstruction of sharp images from these blurred event streams.

The work combines a reconstruction architecture with an event-based model of an out-of-focus camera. A simulator uses that model to create realistic defocused event streams for training and testing. The architecture includes a temporal information encoder, a blur-aware decoder with two branches, and a reconstruction and re-defocus module for learning to correct the blur.

Experiments use both simulated and real-world data, spanning different lighting conditions and blur sizes. The authors report that EvFocus outperforms existing methods across these conditions. The results support handling lens defocus explicitly in event-based imaging, with the camera model and simulator supplying data tailored to the reconstruction problem.
icml-2025-evfocus-learning-to-reconstruc.tldr: EvFocus combines event-camera modeling and a blur-aware network to reconstruct sharp images from out-of-focus event streams.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning seeks to remove particular training examples’ influence from a model. This paper studies malicious unlearning requests that exploit the removal process. The authors identify three problems with existing attacks: fixed targets restrict flexibility, multiple requests are inefficient to handle, and non-convex loss functions can make attack behavior unstable.

Their method, DDPA, uses geometric approximations to address these problems. A convex polyhedral approximation, motivated by Carathéodory’s theorem, identifies locations in the loss landscape where convexity approximately holds. The method uses those locations to support stable attack performance. A second component detects regular simplices, drawing on simplex theory and John’s theorem to maximize coverage of the parameter space.

The authors theoretically derive the proportion of the effective parameter space covered by the constructed simplex. They also evaluate attack success rates on real datasets against state-of-the-art unlearning attacks. The contribution combines a geometric account of where attacks can operate with a method intended to improve flexibility, efficiency, and stability; the abstract does not state a numerical success-rate advantage.
icml-2025-flexible-efficient-and-stable-.tldr: DDPA uses geometric approximations to make adversarial machine-unlearning requests more flexible, efficient, and stable.

paragraphs: Pretrained models can help detect cardiovascular disease from electrocardiograms when labeled data are scarce. Their size, however, makes both adaptation and subsequent prediction expensive on devices with limited resources. H-Tuning addresses these two stages together, aiming to retain useful detection performance while reducing the computational demands of using pretrained models.

The framework first applies H-Tuning to adapt a pretrained model to a downstream ECG dataset at lower cost. It then uses knowledge distillation to reduce the cost of running the resulting model. Treating fine-tuning and inference as separate targets within one framework matters because saving resources during training alone does not resolve deployment costs.

Experiments on four ECG datasets report a 6.34-fold reduction in fine-tuning GPU memory use with detection performance comparable to standard fine-tuning. With distillation, inference latency and memory consumption fall by factors of 4.52 and 19.83, respectively. These results demonstrate substantial computational savings in the evaluated settings and support a route toward ECG detection models that fit tighter resource budgets.
icml-2025-h-tuning-toward-low-cost-and-e.tldr: H-Tuning combines efficient adaptation and knowledge distillation to reduce ECG model training and inference costs while retaining comparable detection performance.

paragraphs: Repeatedly training language models on their own generated text can gradually degrade performance, a phenomenon called model collapse. This paper investigates how the proportion of synthetic training data affects learning and whether a different way of producing synthetic material can avoid that deterioration. Its proposed alternative begins with human-written text.

The authors pretrain models using different synthetic-data proportions and observe that larger proportions correlate with worse performance. Their statistical analysis identifies distribution shifts and excessive concentration of n-gram features, or recurring token sequences. Motivated by these findings, they generate semi-synthetic data by editing tokens in human-produced material instead of relying entirely on self-generated text.

As a theoretical proof of concept, the paper shows that token-level editing can prevent collapse by keeping test error beneath a finite upper bound. Experiments cover training from scratch, continued pretraining, and supervised fine-tuning, reporting improved data quality and model performance. The theoretical result establishes a possibility, while the experiments support the approach across these tested training settings.
icml-2025-how-to-synthesize-text-data-wi.tldr: Editing tokens in human-written text produces semi-synthetic training data that can avoid model collapse and improve performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Models used for database operations can lose accuracy as updates change the data and the relationships they learned. Repeated retraining or fine-tuning adds overhead. FLAIR addresses this concept drift by changing the context supplied to a prediction model at runtime, allowing adaptation without optimizing the model’s parameters during operation.

The framework uses a useful feature of database systems: execution results become available immediately after predictions are acted on. These results support a dynamic context memory that informs subsequent predictions. A Task Featurization Module converts task-specific information into standardized representations, while a Dynamic Decision Engine, pretrained through Bayesian meta-training, uses the changing context to adapt its decisions.

Experiments across database tasks report stronger results than state-of-the-art baselines, including adaptation that is up to 5.2 times faster and a 22.5% error reduction for cardinality estimation. The findings support using current execution feedback as an adaptation mechanism. The reported speed advantage concerns the tested settings, while the underlying design avoids runtime parameter optimization.
icml-2025-in-context-adaptation-to-conce.tldr: FLAIR adapts learned database operations to changing data through execution-informed context, without updating model parameters at runtime.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether two models were trained independently from separate random initializations. It develops two approaches that trade statistical guarantees against flexibility. The question concerns model lineage: detecting whether models, or particular components within them, share a training origin.

In the constrained setting, assumptions about architecture and training allow tests with exact p-values for independent initialization. The tests simulate exchangeable model copies and compare their similarities with those of the original pair. Across 210 pairs drawn from 21 open-weight models, the authors report identifying every non-independent pair.

The unconstrained test matches hidden activations and handles architecture changes and output-preserving transformations intended to evade detection. It no longer provides exact p-values, but empirically distinguishes non-independent models and identifies shared components. Examples include pruning relationships between Llama models and shared layers between Mistral and StripedHyena. The test also withstands retraining individual layers from scratch. Its broader applicability therefore comes with a different evidential status: empirical reliability rather than the constrained test’s exact statistical guarantee.
icml-2025-independence-tests-for-languag.tldr: Two model-lineage tests offer either exact p-values under assumptions or broader empirical detection through hidden-activation matching.

paragraphs: Translating medical image volumes requires capturing relationships throughout three-dimensional space, but learning directly with 3D voxel representations can demand substantial computation and data. Score-Fusion builds a volumetric model by combining 2D diffusion models trained along perpendicular orientations. It combines them in score-function space, using their learned information to support 3D translation.

The model starts from an average of the 2D models, turning 3D training into a fine-tuning process. Its hierarchical layers are also designed to learn combinations of 2D features. These choices reduce the demands of learning volumetric structure. The framework can additionally combine diffusion models conditioned on different inputs, supporting multiple input modalities.

Experiments report superior accuracy and volumetric fidelity for medical image super-resolution and modality translation. The authors also demonstrate the importance of 3D representations for downstream recognition, including tumor segmentation. An extension combines diffusion models on time-space slices with a spatial-temporal video backbone for video super-resolution, showing the approach’s potential beyond medical volumes.
icml-2025-introducing-3d-representation-.tldr: Score-Fusion combines perpendicular 2D diffusion models into an efficient 3D representation for medical volume translation and related tasks.

paragraphs: Adapting very large language models remains expensive even with parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA. LowRA tackles the memory demands of this adaptation by enabling LoRA fine-tuning at less than two bits per parameter. The aim is to compress numerical representations aggressively while keeping the resulting performance loss small.

The framework optimizes several parts of fine-grained quantization: how values are mapped to compressed representations, how thresholds are chosen, and how precision is assigned. It also uses efficient CUDA kernels to support scalable execution. These components address both the numerical quality of compression and the computation needed to use the compressed model.

Evaluations span four language models and four datasets. The authors report a better performance–precision trade-off above two bits, continued accuracy down to 1.15 bits, and memory reductions of up to 50%. These findings support the feasibility of very low-bit LoRA fine-tuning in the evaluated settings, offering a route to adapting large models under tighter memory budgets.
icml-2025-lowra-accurate-and-efficient-l.tldr: LowRA enables accurate LoRA fine-tuning below two bits per parameter, with reported memory savings of up to 50%.

paragraphs: Context-enhanced learning adds information to the context used during ordinary gradient-based language-model training. The additional material is available to the model, but no autoregressive gradients are computed on that material itself. The paper formalizes this arrangement as a gradient-based counterpart to in-context learning and studies why it can help.

For a multi-step reasoning task in a simplified setting, the authors prove that context-enhanced learning can require exponentially fewer samples than standard learning when the model is capable of in-context learning. They attribute the benefit to a more accurate gradient learning signal. The result is conditional on that capability and the analyzed setting, rather than a universal efficiency guarantee.

The paper also experimentally investigates whether the extra contextual learning material can be detected or recovered afterward. It finds that doing so appears difficult. This suggests possible data-security and copyright implications: material can influence gradient-based learning through its role in context, even when it is not itself the target of autoregressive training.
icml-2025-on-the-power-of-context-enhanc.tldr: In a simplified reasoning setting, extra training context can yield exponential sample-efficiency gains when a model can learn in context.

paragraphs: An Internet agent needs a broad range of skills, but manually writing instructions for every skill limits how much training can scale. Proposer-Agent-Evaluator, or PAE, organizes learning around automatically generated tasks and automatically assessed attempts. Its aim is to let agents discover and practice useful behavior on websites.

A context-aware proposer first examines website information and generates task instructions. The agent attempts those tasks, producing interaction trajectories. A vision-language model then evaluates whether each attempt succeeded. Those evaluations become reward signals for reinforcement learning, connecting task creation, practice, and policy improvement in one learning system.

The authors evaluate PAE on vision-based web navigation using real-world and self-hosted websites from WebVoyager and WebArena. They report approximately 50% relative improvement in zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks and websites. This is a relative gain in the evaluated capability, not a percentage-point increase. The findings support autonomously generated practice as a way to expand web-agent skills beyond a fixed collection of human-written instructions.
icml-2025-proposer-agent-evaluator-pae-a.tldr: PAE lets web agents generate tasks, practice them, and learn from automated success judgments, improving generalization in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A diffusion model that reconstructs a graph accurately does not necessarily learn the most useful representation for recognizing its properties. This paper examines that mismatch between generation and representation learning. Its spectral analysis shows that minimizing reconstruction mean squared error need not optimize the information used by downstream tasks.

The authors find that emphasizing a smaller set of features carrying global information can produce stronger representations. Their Smooth Diffusion Model for Graphs, or SDMG, uses a multi-scale smoothing loss and low-frequency information encoders. These components encourage reconstruction of global, low-frequency structure while suppressing high-frequency variation treated as irrelevant noise.

The approach changes which reconstruction errors the learning process emphasizes, connecting the training objective more closely to the desired representation. Extensive experiments support its effectiveness for graph representation learning. The findings suggest that diffusion models’ reconstruction ability can be more useful for recognition when the objective prioritizes relevant structure; they do not establish that minimizing ordinary reconstruction error always produces poor representations.
icml-2025-sdmg-smoothing-your-diffusion-.tldr: SDMG improves graph representations by directing diffusion reconstruction toward global, low-frequency information.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning networks can become less able to learn as training proceeds. Early experiences may dominate later learning, and inactive neurons can reduce the capacity to acquire new knowledge. Resetting networks or neurons can help, but the authors identify high computational costs and inadequate recovery of existing knowledge as problems with earlier reset approaches.

The paper introduces neuron regeneration, which combines resetting with knowledge recovery. Its Sustainable Backup Propagation framework uses scheduled cycle resets to renew neurons and inner distillation to restore knowledge at the neuron level. Together, these procedures support regeneration across the network while addressing the disruption caused by renewal.

The authors integrate the framework with Proximal Policy Optimization and introduce a distillation function for this setting. The resulting algorithm, Plastic PPO, cyclically regenerates all neurons in the actor network. Experiments report that the method preserves policy plasticity and improves sample efficiency. The findings support treating renewal and recovery as linked operations when maintaining an agent’s ability to keep learning.
icml-2025-stay-hungry-keep-learning-sust.tldr: Plastic PPO combines scheduled neuron resets with knowledge recovery to preserve learning capacity and improve sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization learns from preferences over complete responses, making it difficult to incorporate rewards assigned to individual tokens. TGDPO develops a way to bring this finer-grained guidance into DPO. The motivation is that different parts of a response should be able to receive different strengths of training guidance.

The authors first decompose sequence-level Proximal Policy Optimization into token-level optimization problems. With token-level reward guidance, they derive a closed-form optimal token policy and its corresponding reward. Combining that reward with the Bradley–Terry preference model produces computable DPO losses. They also propose a practical guidance mechanism based on DPO’s induced reward.

The formulation lets individual tokens deviate from the reference policy by different amounts according to their rewards. Experiments report win-rate improvements over DPO of up to 7.5 points on MT-Bench, 6.2 points on AlpacaEval 2, and 4.3 points on Arena-Hard. These results support translating fine-grained reward information into preference optimization rather than applying the same response-level guidance uniformly across tokens.
icml-2025-tgdpo-harnessing-token-level-r.tldr: TGDPO incorporates token-level reward guidance into DPO, allowing finer-grained policy changes and improving reported benchmark win rates.

paragraphs: Provenance graphs record how data move through a computer system and how activities depend on one another. These relationships provide useful evidence for intrusion detection, but the graphs can be difficult to store, represent, and analyze at scale. This paper develops a learned baseline of system behavior to make those graphs more useful for anomaly detection.

The method combines dynamic graph processing with adaptive encoding to produce compact embeddings. It addresses previously unseen, or out-of-vocabulary, elements and adjusts to shifts in normal behavior. These capabilities matter because the system’s activities and the meaning of normal operation can change over time.

The learned baseline is then incorporated into a tag-propagation framework for real-time detection. Evaluation supports the method’s accuracy and adaptability in finding anomalous paths through provenance graphs, and the authors report an advance over the state of the art. The contribution connects efficient graph representation with a detection process that uses the recorded relationships among system activities.
icml-2025-the-case-for-learned-provenanc.tldr: An adaptive learned baseline compresses changing provenance graphs and supports real-time detection of anomalous activity paths.

paragraphs: Predicting motion in three dimensions is increasingly relevant to systems that act in physical environments. This paper contributes 3DMoTraj, a dataset collected from unmanned underwater vehicles operating in ocean environments. The dataset is designed specifically for studying 3D trajectory prediction, addressing the absence of such dedicated resources identified by the authors.

The method addresses the added mathematical complexity of moving from two-dimensional to three-dimensional prediction. It first decouples correlations between coordinate axes to produce coarse predictions with reduced complexity. A second stage models those inter-axis correlations to refine the initial predictions. Dependencies are therefore handled explicitly during refinement after the simpler initial prediction stage.

The authors analyze prediction complexity and evaluate the method through extensive experiments. They report significant improvements in 3D trajectory accuracy and performance above state-of-the-art methods. The work contributes both a dedicated source of underwater motion data and a prediction strategy that separates manageable initial estimation from correction based on relationships between axes.
icml-2025-three-dimensional-trajectory-p.tldr: 3DMoTraj provides underwater vehicle trajectories and a two-stage method that simplifies 3D prediction before restoring inter-axis relationships.

paragraphs: Diffusion bridges connect distributions through processes with fixed endpoints and have shown promise for image translation and restoration. Existing approaches can nevertheless produce blurred or overly smooth details. UniDB develops a stochastic optimal control formulation to explain and generalize these models, connecting the transformation process to an explicit optimization objective.

The framework derives a closed-form optimal controller. It shows that diffusion bridges based on Doob’s h-transform arise as a special case when the terminal penalty coefficient grows without bound. Allowing that coefficient to remain tunable creates a way to balance the cost of controlling the process against the penalty associated with its endpoint.

The authors report that this balance improves detail preservation and output quality. UniDB can be incorporated into existing diffusion bridge models with minimal code changes, and experiments across image restoration tasks support its performance and adaptability. The contribution is both theoretical and practical: a shared formulation explains existing bridges while exposing a parameter that can improve their restoration behavior.
icml-2025-unidb-a-unified-diffusion-brid.tldr: UniDB unifies diffusion bridges through stochastic optimal control and uses a tunable endpoint penalty to improve image detail preservation.

paragraphs: Preference feedback can serve as a proxy for what a model should actually achieve, but optimizing that proxy may fail to improve the true objective. This paper asks when proxy feedback can still help if a small amount of expert data is available. The focus is on learning the ground-truth policy more efficiently.

The authors give sufficient conditions on proxy feedback under which adding proxy data provably improves sample complexity, meaning the amount of data needed for learning. These conditions describe a route to a benefit; they are not presented as necessary conditions that all useful proxies must satisfy. They can also inform how feedback is collected for particular tasks.

The theoretical result implies a language-model parameterization that achieves the improved sample complexity, and the paper explains how existing architectures can be adapted accordingly. Its contribution is a conditional account of when imperfect feedback helps, linking assumptions about that feedback to a learning design with a provable data-efficiency advantage.
icml-2025-when-can-proxies-improve-the-s.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions under which proxy preferences, combined with sparse expert data, provably reduce the data needed to learn the true policy.
